analysis.one_liner: Restores broad disability discrimination protections narrowed by Supreme Court rulings.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee or House floor vote before the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: Courts, including the Supreme Court, had read the Americans with Disabilities Act narrowly, ruling that many people whose conditions are controlled by medication or devices no longer count as disabled and cannot sue over discrimination. This bill would rewrite the ADA's definition of disability so that using medication, hearing aids, or other mitigating measures does not erase your protection, and so that people treated as disabled are covered too. It also told courts to read the law broadly. The bill died in committee without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People with disabilities — including workers whose diabetes, epilepsy, cancer, hearing loss, or other conditions are managed with medication or devices — would regain the ability to sue employers and businesses that discriminate against them. People treated as disabled even without an impairment would also be protected.

how_it_helps.text: The bill states that courts, including the Supreme Court, have significantly limited the reach of the ADA, leaving many people with actual or perceived impairments subject to discrimination, and declares it necessary to restore the law's original intent.

It would change the definition of disability so that a person's use of mitigating measures — medication, prosthetics, or other treatments — is not counted when deciding whether they have an impairment, and so that episodic, short-term, or long-term impairments all qualify.

It would add explicit definitions of physical impairment, mental impairment, a record of impairment, and a perceived impairment, covering people who are discriminated against because they are treated as disabled even if they are not.
It would direct that the ADA be broadly construed to advance its remedial purpose of a comprehensive prohibition on disability discrimination.

analysis.who_pays: Employers would face broader exposure to discrimination lawsuits and more accommodation obligations, including for workers whose conditions are fully controlled by treatment. Businesses would bear the costs of litigation and compliance.

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection is cost and uncertainty for employers: dropping the requirement that an impairment substantially limit a major life activity, and ignoring mitigating measures, would sweep in millions of workers with common, well-controlled conditions and likely increase litigation.

The bill leaves the qualified-individual defense intact, so employers could still argue a worker cannot perform essential job functions, but deciding who is qualified would become more contested as more people qualify as disabled.
Small businesses with limited legal and HR resources would bear a disproportionate share of the new compliance burden compared with large corporations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the tens of millions of Americans with disabilities, the benefit is substantial: restoring the civil rights protections courts had stripped away. The cost falls on employers, in litigation risk and accommodation duties, and critics argued the draft was broader than necessary. Disability advocates and business groups later negotiated a narrower version that became law in 2008, which suggests this draft was written at the outer edge of what stakeholders could accept.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late September 2006, referred to four committees, and sent to two subcommittees, and the Congress ended in early January 2007 with no markup, no floor vote, and no Senate action.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 29, 2006, near the end of the 109th Congress, by Rep. Sensenbrenner with Reps. Hoyer and Conyers, and referred to four House committees.

On October 2, 2006, it was referred to the Health Subcommittee, and on November 2, 2006, to the Employer-Employee Relations Subcommittee, where it sat; the record shows no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action before the Congress ended on January 3, 2007.
Only two additional cosponsors signed on during the bill's brief life.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers are better off, because the narrowed, court-imposed reading of the ADA stayed in force through the end of the Congress. Disability advocates eventually won the change two years later, when a negotiated successor, the ADA Amendments Act of 2008, became law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, until a successor passed in 2008

for.name: Rep. F. James Sensenbrenner Jr.
for.role: House Judiciary Committee chairman; lead sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: Rep. John Conyers Jr.
for.role: Ranking member, House Judiciary Committee; original co-introducer

against.name: House Education and Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and sent it to the Employer-Employee Relations Subcommittee on November 2, 2006; never held a markup or voted on it before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Judiciary, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Energy and Commerce Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no recorded action on it.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and allied business groups
against.what_they_did: Opposed broad expansion of ADA liability and pressed for a narrower rewrite of the disability definition; the eventual 2008 law was negotiated with business input.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was led by a senior Republican (Sensenbrenner) with two top House Democrats (Hoyer and Conyers), and its only two cosponsors were Democrats; nothing in the record shows party-line opposition, but no committee or floor vote ever occurred to test it.

industries.note: The bill would have broadened who can sue for disability discrimination by disregarding mitigating measures and covering perceived impairments, expanding employers' litigation and accommodation costs. Its interest in blocking the bill ran directly against the workers the bill would protect.
Broader ADA claims mean more work for lawyers defending employers; this effect cuts in favor of more litigation rather than either workers or businesses as a whole.
